idiom_name: hand-rolled Trampoline<T> interface with done/more and a jump loop
implementation_notes: The JVM provides no general tail-call elimination, so the canonical Java form is the hand-written Trampoline<T> hierarchy from the Java Design Patterns catalog: a functional interface whose completed instances return the value, and a suspended form whose Supplier yields the next Trampoline, driven by a loop (Stream.iterate(t, Trampoline::jump).filter(Trampoline::complete).findFirst() is the catalog's driver; a while loop is cheaper). Recursive methods return Trampoline<T> instead of calling each other. Virtual threads do not help, because they change scheduling, not frame depth. Keep the recursive form while depth is bounded by the data model.
pitfalls: Every step allocates a lambda plus a Trampoline object, and the Stream.iterate driver adds an iterator chain on top; a while loop is the allocation-light driver.
Checked exceptions cannot travel through Supplier or the step sum type, so they must be wrapped or recorded in the step value, and the logical frames are absent from the stack trace.
Virtual threads and structured concurrency do not remove per-call frames: they multiplex execution, not stack depth.
